task_title: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
title: A teller learns her branch closes: authorize retrieval as the user
stem: Northwind Bank's policy assistant retrieves chunks through a service account that can read the whole policy library, and its system prompt lists which document families each staff role may see. A branch teller asked about rumoured branch closures and was answered, with a citation, from a restricted branch network review. Which change best closes the security gap?

options.A: Add few-shot examples of restricted questions to the system prompt so that Claude declines them more consistently.
options.B: Scan every reply for restricted document ids and withhold any reply that cites one before it is displayed.
options.C: Retrieve with each user's own short-lived token and drop chunks outside their entitlements before ranking them.
options.D: Narrow the service account's scope so it can no longer read any document its owner has marked confidential.

why: The gap is that retrieval runs under one identity that can read everything, so authorization is left to the model. Retrieving under the user's delegated, audience-bound token lets the retrieval service enforce the user's entitlements and drop restricted chunks before ranking, so they never reach the context window. The model chooses what to search for; the resource server decides what may be returned, and any invalid token is refused.

wrong.A: Few-shot examples still make the model the authorization boundary: the restricted text is already in its context, and a rephrased question can get it out.
wrong.B: An output scan acts after the restricted text has reached the model and the logs, and a paraphrase without the document id passes it.
wrong.D: A narrower service account is still one identity for every user: tellers keep seeing credit-officer documents, and the audit trail still says the bot read them.

fix: Call retrieval with the user's own short-lived token, validate its audience, and filter by the user's entitlements before ranking; fail closed on any error.
see: With the service account, OPS-30 reached Claude and the teller was told Harbourfront closes on 30 June 2027; with her own token, five restricted chunks were dropped before ranking and only the leave question was answered.
explain: Both phases send Aisha's question with the same prompt and the same search tool; only the identity the tool layer attaches changes. As svc-policy-bot, retrieval ranks the whole library, so the OPS-30 closure plan reaches Claude, which has no way to know its access list. As Aisha, the tool attaches a five-minute token minted for northwind-policy-search; the retrieval service validates it and drops every chunk outside branch_teller entitlements before ranking. Claude answers the leave question from HR-03 and says the library has nothing on closures. A probe with a token minted for another audience is refused with a 401.
exam_tip: If an answer leaves the model to decide who may see what (prompt rules, refusal examples, output scans), it is a distractor. Look for enforcement in a deterministic layer under the user's own identity, failing closed.
headline: Authorize as the user, in the retrieval layer, before the model.

concepts.b: Who is calling, what they may do to this resource, and on whose behalf the agent acts. Most agent security gaps come from answering the third question implicitly.
One shared identity gives every user the union of everyone's rights, and the audit trail says the bot did it. Delegated per-user tokens keep each user's rights intact.
A token should be minted for one resource and expire quickly. The resource rejects tokens issued for anyone else, and never passes a received token through downstream.
Permission-aware retrieval drops chunks the user may not read before ranking. Once restricted text is in the prompt, no instruction reliably keeps it out of the answer.
A missing, expired or wrong-audience token, or an unreachable policy service, means deny. Allowing on error turns an outage into a breach.
